background.definition: The OSA syndrome, or OSAHS, is defined as abnormal breathing patterns during sleep that cause recurrent arousals (often without complete awakening, fragmentation of sleep, and hypoxemia), resulting in excessive daytime sleepiness.

list.listitem: The Wisconsin Sleep Cohort Study estimates at least mild OSA has a prevalence of 24% in men and 5% in women. Associated excessive daytime sleepiness was present in only 4% and 2%, respectively.
There is a variation in prevalence among ethnic groups, and little is known of prevalence in resource-poor countries.
Up to 12 million Americans have OSAHS, and 10 million remain undiagnosed.
One small study suggests that treatment of OSA with nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) prevents car accidents.

Apnea is the complete cessation of airflow through the upper airway for a period of 10 seconds, while the more common hypopnea is a 30% to 50% reduction of airflow or thoracoabdominal movement for the same period, with at least a 4% oxygen desaturation index (ODI).
The primary measure of severity is the average sum of apneic or hypopneic events experienced per hour, expressed as the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) or respiratory disturbance index.
Highly associated with obesity, but normal weight individuals are also susceptible.
A diagnosis of OSA should be considered for any complaint of excessive daytime sleepiness. C
Excessive weight gain can predispose patients to development of OSA. C

The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of routine screening for the disorder, but consideration of the diagnosis during routine medical care is prudent when complaints of daytime sleepiness are prominent.

A screening tool for OSA in obese patients regardleess of presence of symptoms was shown to be 83% accuracy and polysomnography, but it is awaiting external validation studies in different patient populations.
Point-of-care ultrasound has shown some promise in detecting anatomic features that predispose to developing OSA.
Obesity is highly correlated with OSA; thus, maintaining a healthy weight may reduce the chances of developing the disorder.
Weight loss
Reduced alcohol consumption
Lateral, not supine, body position during sleep
Good sleep hygiene
Individuals with obesity or overweight
Individuals with large neck circumference
Male gender or postmenopausal females
Craniofacial abnormalities or other conditions predisposing to a narrowed upper airway
Increasing age
Endocrinopathies (e.g., hypothyroidism, acromegaly)

A Cochrane review found no evidence that opioid, hypnotic, and sedating medications have adverse effects on the severity of OSA, based on changes in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) and oxygen desaturation index (ODI). However, minimum overnight peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (SpO2) was statistically lower and clinically impaired among patients on remifentanil (an opioid), zolpidem, and triazolam.
Attended polysomnography is the diagnostic gold standard for OSA. C
Ambulatory automatically titrated PAP (APAP) with oximetry is a diagnostic alternative when the pretest probability is high and polysomnography is not readily available. C

list.listitem: Severity of OSA is usually defined by the AHI determined from polysomnography.
There is no universally accepted standard; but the American Academy of Sleep Medicine defines mild disease as an AHI of 5 to 15, moderate as 15 to 30, and severe as 30 or more.
Diagnosis of OSA syndrome requires the presence of excessive daytime sleepiness.
The presenting signs and symptoms of OSA are nonspecific. A complaint of excessive daytime sleepiness, especially with impairment of driving or executive functioning, should raise clinical suspicion.

Those signs and symptoms that predispose patients to this diagnosis include intense snoring, observed choking during sleep, driving impairment, increased body mass index, male gender, and increasing age. The more of these factors that are present, the greater the likelihood of a positive sleep study.

Physical exam findings associated with OSA include: modified Mallampati score 3 to 4, retrognathia, macroglossia, tonsilalr hypertrophy, elongated or enlarged uvula, nasal abnormalities, high-arched or narrow hard palate.
In one study, the "elbow sign" (being poked or elbowed in the ribs by one's bed partner for snoring or interrupted breathing) had reasonable correlation with an abnormal polysomnogram result.

The findings that are most helpful at ruling in disease are awakening with choking/gasping, hypertension, large neck circumference (collar size >17 inches in men), and dress size >19 in women. Similarly, a recent systematic review found that nocturnal gasping or choking was the strongest historical indicator of OSA, while snoring was not very helpful.
Resistant hypertension and/or atrial fibrillation also correlates with OSA.
Attended polysomnography (sleep study) is the diagnostic standard for OSA.

Multichannel portable home monitoring is an alternative testing strategy for those with a high pretest probability for the disorder. In this case, desaturation events of more than 4% at a rate greater than 15 per hour carries a high LR+.
Home testing is recommended by VA guidelines as the initial test, followed by repeat home testing or sleep lab polysomnography if non-diagnostic.

Patients with a high pretest probability of moderate-to-severe OSA can be diagnosed and initially managed using ambulatory APAP titration and overnight oximetry instead of attended polysomnography. This strategy may also increase adherence to treatment.

Point-of-care ultrasound has shown some promise in detecting anatomic features that predispose to developing OSA. Specific features include distance between lingual arteries >30 mm; mean resting tongue thickness >60 mm; and a combination of neck circumference and retropalatal (RP) diameter shortening during the Muller maneuver.

A clinical decision rule based on the history and physical may be of some assistance in determining a higher chance of diagnosing the disorder. The STOP questions (Snoring/Tiredness/Observed stopped breathing/blood Pressure) are recommended by VA guidelines. Other externally validated screening tools include the Sleep Apnea Clinical Score and the STOP-BANG questionnaire (which add Body mass index, Age, Neck size, and Gender) but are no more accurate than the STOP questions alone.

A study found that a score of 5 points or higher on a 10-point scale (3 points for bothersome snoring, 3 points for waist circumference >102 cm in men or >88 cm in women, 2 points for age >50 years, 3 points for cessation of breathing during sleep), plus at least 3% desaturation on a home oxygen monitor, had a 96% negative predictive value and 56% positive predictive value for OSA in a prospective validation group.

The Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) does not correlate well with the severity of the AHI; however, it is often a requirement of health insurers that patients have a certain minimum score before they will cover a sleep study.

A nasal delivery system for PAP is the first-line choice for treatment.B
It is appropriate to recommend oral appliances (OAs) to those with mild symptomatic OSA or to those unable to tolerate nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). B
CPAP improves sleepiness symptoms and quality-of-life scores in patients with moderate-to-severe OSAHS. A
Tirzepatide significantly improved symptoms and the apnea hypopnea index in patients with sleep apnea who are obese.B
There is no demonstrated overall significant long-term benefit to surgery for treatment of OSA. B

Two parallel studies randomized 469 persons with obstructive sleep apnea to tirzepatide 2.5 mg once weekly, titrated to 10 to 15 mg once weekly, or placebo. The baseline apnea hypopnea index (AHI) was approximately 50 in both studies, and decreased by 20 to 24 points more in the treatment groups than in controls. Body weight also decreased 16% to 17%. GI events were more common with tirzepatide.
Canadian national guideline on pharmacotherapy for the treatment of obesity recommends tirzepatide or liraglutide for patients with obesity and sleep apnea.
Previous studies have not identified any other medication with consistent improved patient-oriented outcomes.
Oral hypnotic medications do not improve adherence with CPAP therapy in men with OSA.
Modafanil may reduce residual daytime sleepiness in patients on nasal CPAP and may also decrease sleepiness after CPAP withdrawal.
Armodafanil may reduce excessive sleepiness in patients on nasal CPAP and in with comorbid depression.

In patients with moderate-to-severe OSA who are unable to tolerate CPAP, implantation of an upper airway device that stimulates the hypoglossal nerve causing anterior tongue displacement, appears to be an effective alternative.

Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, laser-assisted uvulopalatoplasty, multilevel temperature-controlled radiofrequency tissue ablation, maxillo-mandibular advancement, genioglossus advancement alone or in combination are used to increase the patency of the airway in hopes of improving the severity of OSA. Some have shown promise for improvement of long-term outcomes, but there is insufficient evidence to suggest routine use.
Surgical intervention should be a last resort, after CPAP or OA, given lack of current evidence of long-term efficacy and risk of surgery.

Behavioral interventions are supported by high-certainty evidence, supportive interventions by moderate-certainty evidence, and educational and mixed interventions by very low-certainty evidence as ways of improving CPAP use among CPAP-naive individuals, albeit modestly.
Support groups for people affected by sleep apnea are available.
Multimodal telemonitoring did not increase CPAP adherence in patients with OSA and elevated CV risk.

CPAP reduces symptoms of sleepiness and improves quality-of-life measures in people with moderate and severe OSA. However, CPAP in patients with OSA but no daytime sleepiness did not reduce hypertension or cardiovascular events in a randomized trial with 5 years of followup.

The combination of CPAP with best supportive treatment appears to decrease central apnea hypopnea index in patients with central sleep apnea from heart failure more than best supportive treatment alone.

Among patients with heart failure, PAP has uncertain effects on all-cause mortality and does not appear to decrease cardiac mortality and rehospitalization. But it may improve quality of life for those with central sleep apnea. There is uncertainty regarding adverse events from PAP compared to usual care.

The use of auto-CPAP (ie, machines that automatically adjust pressure settings to increase comfort) likely lengthens duration of use by 13 mintues at night but does not have clinically meaningful impact on daytime sleepiness among patients with moderate to severe OSA.
Despite correlations between hepatic steatosis and OSA severity, use of CPAP did not improve hepatic steatosis or fibrosis in patients with NAFLD.
A randomized trial with 109 patients found that CPAP does not reduce the percent time in atrial fibrillation.
Nasal CPAP is the most effective PAP interface initially, but alternatives may be required for patient intolerance. Oxygen therapy is not recommended by VA guidelines.
The benefit of CPAP for those with mild OSA may not outweigh the subjective inconvenience.
For men with OSA and erectile dysfunction (ED), it is unclear if using CPAP improves ED.

Oral appliances for mandibular advancement may be effective in reducing subjective sleepiness and sleep-disordered breathing, but less so than CPAP.However, a randomized controlled trial of OA in 96 adults with mild-to-moderate OSA did not find improvements in daytime sleepiness or quality of life.
OA is more appropriate for mild OSA and those unwilling or unable to tolerate CPAP. OA is more effective at 12 months than surgical intervention in reducing the severity of OSA.
OA is minimally effective, if at all, for edentulous patients and those with dentures.
OA is not recommended for patients more than 150% of their ideal body weight (too much redundant tissue collapsing airway).
An RCT found no difference between heat molded and custom made OA's for OSA.
For patients who are overweight, a randomized trial found that assignment to a weight loss group decreases AHI more than usual care.

A systematic review of 9 RCTs involving 444 patients concluded that exercise improves OSA severity but not BMI, and that a combination of aerobic exercise and resistance training is superior to aerobic exercise alone in reducing AHI.
For patients with positional OSA, use of a forehead vibrating device led to a 30% reduction in AHI with increased total sleep time.

A Cochrane review found CPAP more effective than positional therapy in improving AHI among patients with positional OSA, but positional therapy has better adherence than CPAP. Additionally, positional therapy appears better than inactive control for improving AHI and ESS scores. No improvement in quality of life or cognitive measures was found.

Myofunctional therapy or oropharyngeal exercises, consisting of mouth and throat exercises, may improve sleep quality and daytime sleepiness in the short term, based on moderate to very low certainty evidence from a Cochrane review of 9 RCTs involving 347 patients.
Treatment duration is for as long as the condition exists, and there is some evidence that OSA worsens with increasing age.
Patients who gain or lose 10% to 15% of their body weight should be re-evaluated with polysomnography for retitration of PAP settings.
Severe, complex, or central OSA merits referral to a sleep physician, as does severe neurologic, cardiovascular, or pulmonary disease.
Difficulties with PAP adherence or craniofacial abnormalities may require referral.
Refer patients for whom reliable wakefulness is a job requirement, such as pilots.

Despite interventions intended to improve compliance with PAP, there is no improvement with APAP, bilevel PAP wherein there are different inspiratory and expiratory pressures applied, or added humidification.
Adherence to therapy is relatively poor, so follow-up for prescribed therapy is necessary to identify and address any barriers to adherence. C
OSA is a significant risk factor for development of refractory hypertension, congestive heart failure (CHF), cardiac arrhythmias, C Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease. A

OSA is a significant risk factor for development of refractory hypertension and is associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, CHF, cardiac arrhythmias (primarily atrial fibrillation), and cerebrovascular disease.
There are few long-term outcome studies for treatment of OSA, so no effect on mortality has yet been demonstrated.
CPAP improves sleepiness and quality-of-life scores in treated patients with moderate-to-severe OSA.
Intensive lifestyle intervention, as compared to diabetes support and education, led to a 12.2% increase in OSA remission in 10 years in patients with DM.

From post hoc analyses of the SAVE trial, self-reported increases in snoring frequency, loudness, or breathing pauses were associated with a significant increase in a primary composite outcome of CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke. This association was highest for cerebrovascular events.
There are reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure in short-term studies, but the persistence of this disease-oriented outcome over the long term is not known.
CPAP in patients with OSA and type 2 diabetes does not improve glycemic control, and does not reduce the likelihood of cardiovascular events in patients with cardiovascular disease.
The effectiveness of PAP therapy in reducing the AHI is documented during the treatment/titration phase of the sleep study.
The effect of treatment on the severity of sleepiness can be documented with readministration of the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS).
Adherence to therapy is relatively poor, with between 50% and 65% of patients continuing to use their PAP device at all, and those patients using it only 4 to 5 hours per night.
Patients who lose 10% to 15% of their body weight should be re-evaluated with polysomnography before continuing treatment with CPAP.

The etiology, clinical presentation, and treatment for children with OSA are frequently quite different from that for adults and are outside the scope of this topic. Refer to the American Thoracic Society (ATS) guidelines for the management of persistent, post-adenotonsillectomy OSA in children.

The guidelines recommend: 1) continuous positive airway pressure for children who are not candidates for or do not respond to site-specific upper airway treatments, 2) consider orthodontic and denofacial orthopedics for children with craniofacial features contributing to OSA, 3) treatment of obesity, 4) and intranasal corticosteroids + optionally montelukast.

In children with snoring and mild sleep apnea, a randomized trial with 458 children age 3 to 12.9 years found no benefit to adenotonsillectomy compared with watchful waiting for improving the 2 primary outcomes of executive function or attention at 12 months. Approximately 3% of children who underwent surgery required additional interventions for perioperative complications, including secondary hemorrhage.
